Tom Mueller, SpaceX employee #1, says Elon Musk reversed his approach to engineering by demanding they find where rocket engines break and then push them harder

"It changed just working with Elon. At my previous company, it was like, you never blow up a rocket engine or fail a rocket engine. That's bad. This is bad karma. Never test, always have a lot of margin and make sure that you don't fail it."

"And Elon's whole thing was, well, let's find out where it breaks and then fix that and go and push it even more. So it's really a whole different way of thinking about it. Really refreshing, and you learn a lot."

"We had things that we thought would break that we couldn't break. Other things would break because the engineering is not always that deterministic. It's not always obvious. I'm amazed that this thing is still running."

quote.author: firesidealpha
quote.name: Fireside Alpha
quote.text:
Joe Rogan reveals he watched a SpaceX launch with Elon Musk from the command center, and says the rockets explode because SpaceX pushes them to the limit on purpose

"It's not just that. It just shows a complete lack of understanding of what he's trying to accomplish. The whole reason why they're exploding is because you're pushing the tolerances. You're pushing it to the limit, and he expects them to explode. And then he finds out what the weak points are."

"I was actually in the command center watching one of the SpaceX launches. So we watched it from the ground. It takes off, and then we go upstairs, and I'm chilling with Elon. That was surreal. You want to talk surreal?"

"You're watching it on, like, a fucking dozen screens as it's flying over Australia, as it goes into the darkness of night on the dark side of the planet, and then it comes over on the other side into the brightness of the sun and then lands in the ocean. It was bananas."

"But they have all these sensors all over the thing, and so they're monitoring the hull, and the hull actually had a problem. It was leaking. So they're like, 'Well, might explode. Might explode.' You know, catastrophically entertaining. But they're doing it on purpose. That is how they find out how these things work."

Elon Musk quickly impressed Franz von Holzhausen, persuading him to join Tesla and leave behind a successful career at Mazda. Franz recalls: "For somebody who's going to put rockets into space, car is actually not that hard, and his vision for the car and his sustainable direction and message is exactly what I'm looking for."

In the summer of 2008, Franz already had the kind of automotive career most designers dream about, having penned sports cars at GM and led design at Mazda North America, while Tesla was near bankruptcy. 

But after meeting Elon Musk at SpaceX and going for a drive together in an early Roadster while people on the street stopped to stare, Franz walked away from his secure job to start designing the Model S from a blank sheet of paper. When he later explained why he took that leap of faith into a startup with no guarantees, his answer came down to Elon's total commitment: "Tesla was all in."

So not only is @elonmusk a super engineer...physicist...and future imaginer...he's also an exceptionally well-prepared entrepreneur.  Which means he can take advantage of financial market disruptions like those now taking place.  To the great benefit of @SpaceX and @Tesla.

Data centers built by others cost on average $60 billion for a gigawatt...take 30 months on average to open...and when they do are often plagued with initial operating problems.  So called neocloud providers build and rent such projects under long-term leases for about $12 billion per year. No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

看看去年黄仁勋亲自飞去 SpaceX 见马斯克的这段视频，这段交情，早就在十年前焊死了。

2016 年，黄仁勋发布全世界第一台 AI 超算 DGX-1。那是当时最顶尖的机器，可发布完，台下一片安静，一张订单都没有。

就凭这一句，那台初代机器被送到了当时的 OpenAI，也顺手点燃了今天的 AI 时代。

11 月 13 日，黄仁勋还在谷底、能否回归毫无定数，马斯克公开站出来签请愿书；

一次产品还没卖出去，一次人还没回去。两次，马斯克都没等结果。

世人习惯等尘埃落定才选边站，顶级强者之间最稀缺的，恰恰是看不清结局时的那次托底。

one assumption i want to question about AI is that we'll eventually figure out the “best future” and then the remaining task will be getting everyone to agree to it. people want different things, and what they want can change. where more intelligence will help is in making those differences easier to accommodate.

nick bostrom's influence is worth revisiting on anthropic's ipo day. dario, like many of today’s most influential ai founders and researchers, read his work over a decade ago, and bostrom’s book superintelligence helped define questions the industry still faces. i'd like us to engage just as seriously with the possibilities bostrom explores in deep utopia, his subsequent book which asks what we do after we get superintelligence. some notes from my conversation with @eddylazzarin:

-superintelligence could make radically different versions of the “good life” possible. you might want a 200-year lifespan and a village where nobody carries a phone; someone else might want neural implants. someone else might want to live in vice city (either the real version or just a super realistic matrix-sim). ai could help design the economic arrangements that sustain all of this.
-there’s a secondary problem though - even when we have beneficial tech, we may lack the will to diffuse it. waymo and GLP-1s, for example, can save lives (neurosurgeons have compared waymo’s safety results to a treatment so effective that continuing to give patients a placebo would become unethical). and yet evidence of a benefit doesn’t automatically produce the will to act on it.
-the reality described in deep utopia ameliorates this by imagining that our psychology might one day become changeable too. i might want an environment that suits my temperament but i can also go the opposite direction and manipulate myself to become more adventurous or less anxious, in other words, more suited to my environment. the interesting possibility is having more agency over both worlds, external and internal. glps’ effect on appetite already suggests how technology can change the effort involved in pursuing a goal (though again, it is telling that not everyone who *should* be on peptides *are* despite the health benefits). the sci-fi version extends that possibility enormously.
-timing matters. bostrom reminds us that people continue to die while potentially lifesaving advances remain unavailable (he literally says “if nobody builds it, everyone dies” as a hypothetical inversion of yudkowsky/soares’ book).

i’d like ai to make it easier for people to live very different lives, without creating this burden of proof that theirs is the best one.

posts.text:
This is f*cking insane. OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever, who left to build his own superintelligence lab, described the long-term future with AI, and admitted he doesn't like it:

"So maybe every person will have an AI that will do their bidding. And that's good"

"Then the AI goes and earns money for the person, and advocates for their needs in the political sphere. And maybe then writes a little report saying, okay, here's what I've done. And the person says, great, keep it up. But the person is no longer a participant"

In 2 minutes, he gives the only answer he sees, and says up front "I don't like the solution, but it is a solution": people "become part AI with some kind of Neuralink++"

An AI for Every Person → It Earns and Speaks for You → You Stop Participating → Part Human, Part AI

The man who built ChatGPT's brain thinks the way to stay in the game is to merge with AI
